directions.description: A meme is a unit of cultural information that replicates through human minds. Model meme propagation as a sheaf over the social network graph: each node is a person, each edge is a communication channel, and the meme is a section of the sheaf that must satisfy consistency conditions at each node. Define meme fitness as the sheaf cohomology group H^1(G, M) where G is the social network and M is the meme sheaf. A meme with H^1 = 0 is universally transmissible (it has no consistency barriers — anyone can understand it). A meme with H^1 of dimension d requires d 'interpretation steps' to cross between communities. Conjecture: The most viral memes have H^1(G, M) = 0 but H^0(G, M) of maximal dimension — they spread everywhere AND mean different things to different communities. The dimension of H^0 counts the number of distinct interpretations. A meme that means the same thing to everyone has dim(H^0) = 1 and dim(H^1) = 0. A meme that means different things to different communities has dim(H^0) > 1 and dim(H^1) = 0. A meme that CANNOT spread between communities has H^1 > 0. Test: model Twitter/X retweet networks as graphs G with 1000 nodes, assign meme sheaves based on community structure, compute H^0 and H^1, and correlate with actual virality data. Impact: meme virality is a topological property — it's not about content quality but about the sheaf cohomology of the social network.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the meme sheaf M on social network G: for each community C_i (cluster in G), M(C_i) is the set of interpretations of the meme in community i. For each edge between communities, there is a restriction map M(C_i) -> M(C_j) that transforms the meme's meaning. Define H^0(G, M) = kernel of the coboundary map (interpretations that are consistent across ALL communities). Define H^1(G, M) = cokernel (obstructions to consistent interpretation). Prove: dim(H^0) = number of universal interpretations. Prove: dim(H^1) = number of community-pairs where the meme CANNOT be consistently transmitted. Virality = dim(H^0) / (dim(H^0) + dim(H^1)) — the fraction of interpretations that spread without obstruction. Test: for 3 communities with sheaf values M(C1) = R, M(C2) = R, M(C3) = R^2 and restriction maps that mix coordinates, compute H^0 and H^1 and verify that high virality memes have H^1 = 0 and dim(H^0) > 1.
directions.title: The Mathematics of Memes: Viral Information Topology

directions.description: Euclid's parallel postulate says parallel lines never meet. Hyperbolic geometry says they can diverge. Elliptic geometry says they converge. But what about a geometry where parallel lines BOTH converge AND diverge? Define a Split Geometry on R^2 where the parallel postulate is direction-dependent: lines parallel to the x-axis diverge (hyperbolic behavior) while lines parallel to the y-axis converge (elliptic behavior). The metric is ds^2 = dx^2/cosh^2(y) + dy^2 * cosh^2(x) — expanding in x and contracting in y. Conjecture: Split Geometry is a consistent Riemannian geometry with curvature K(x,y) = -sech^2(y) + sech^2(x) that changes sign across the diagonals. The geometry has a 'phase boundary' along the lines y = x and y = -x where K = 0 (flat). In the region |x| > |y|, K > 0 (elliptic) and in the region |y| > |x|, K < 0 (hyperbolic). The geodesics in split geometry are piecewise combinations of exponential curves (in hyperbolic regions) and trigonometric curves (in elliptic regions). Test: compute the Christoffel symbols and curvature tensor for the split metric. Prove that geodesics cross the phase boundary at most twice. Compute the area of a split triangle with one vertex in each region. Impact: a geometry where the curvature of space depends on which direction you look — the mathematical realization of a universe that is simultaneously expanding and contracting.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the split metric g = diag(1/cosh^2(y), cosh^2(x)) on R^2. Compute the Christoffel symbols: Gamma^1_{11} = tanh(y), Gamma^1_{12} = 0, Gamma^1_{22} = -sinh(x)cosh(x), Gamma^2_{11} = -tanh(y)*cosh^2(x)*cosh^2(y), Gamma^2_{12} = 0, Gamma^2_{22} = -sinh(x)cosh(x). Compute curvature: K = -sech^2(y) + sech^2(x). Verify: K = 0 on y = x and y = -x. K > 0 for |x| > |y| (elliptic). K < 0 for |y| > |x| (hyperbolic). Prove geodesic crossing: a geodesic that enters the elliptic region and then the hyperbolic region crosses the flat boundary at most twice (by convexity of the curvature sign along the geodesic). Compute split triangle area: integral of sqrt(det(g)) = integral of cosh(x)/cosh(y) over the triangle. Test: numerical verification for specific triangles.
directions.title: Impossible Geometries: Where Parallel Lines Converge AND Diverge

directions.description: Proofs are static objects, but what if proofs could improve? Define a proof refinement system where each proof P has a complexity C(P) = length(P) + depth(P) + number of lemmas, and a proof P' is a refinement of P if P' proves the same theorem with C(P') < C(P). Conjecture: For every theorem T provable in ZFC, there exists a sequence of refinements P = P_0, P_1, P_2, ... such that C(P_n) is non-increasing and the limit P_infinity is the simplest proof of T (in the sense of Kolmogorov complexity). Moreover, the refinement process halts: there exists N such that C(P_N) = C(P_{N+1}) = ... = C(P_infinity). The key insight: proof simplification is a well-founded process because the complexity is a natural number that decreases at each step. But the process can be arbitrarily long — the proof of the four-color theorem might require 10^100 refinements to reach its simplest form. Test: formalize the refinement system in Lean 4. Starting from the statement of the irrationality of sqrt(2), generate refinements by eliminating unnecessary lemmas, shortening case splits, and removing redundant quantifiers. Measure C(P) at each step and verify it decreases. Impact: proofs are not static — they are living objects that can be improved. The simplest proof of a theorem is the LIMIT of the refinement process, and this limit ALWAYS exists.
directions.proof_strategy: Define proof complexity C(P) = length(P) + depth(P) + number_of_lemmas(P) for a proof P in a formal system. Define refinement: P' refines P if P' proves the same theorem as P and C(P') < C(P). Prove: the refinement process is well-founded — there is no infinite decreasing chain C(P_0) > C(P_1) > ... because C takes values in the natural numbers. Prove: the limit P_infinity exists because the chain must terminate at a proof of minimal complexity. Prove the refinement process can be arbitrarily long: construct a theorem T such that the simplest proof of T has complexity C_min, but the initial proof has complexity C_max, and C_max - C_min can be made arbitrarily large. Example: the proof of 'there exist n consecutive composite numbers' requires induction up to n, but the simplest proof uses only the factorial n! + 2, n! + 3, ..., n! + n. Test: implement refinement for sqrt(2) irrationality in Lean 4.
directions.title: Self-Improving Proofs: Proofs That Get Simpler Over Time

directions.description: L-functions are the DNA of mathematics — each one encodes deep arithmetic information. But how many L-functions ARE there? The L-function universe is vast: (1) The Riemann zeta function (1 L-function), (2) Dirichlet L-functions (countably many), (3) L-functions of elliptic curves (uncountably many, one per j-invariant), (4) L-functions of modular forms (countably many, but indexed by weight and level), (5) L-functions of Galois representations (enormous family). Conjecture: The set of 'natural' L-functions (those satisfying the Selberg class axioms: analytic continuation, functional equation, Euler product, Ramanujan bound) is COUNTABLE. This means the universe of well-behaved L-functions is no bigger than the integers, despite each individual L-function encoding infinitely much information. The Selberg class is a universe of countable stars, each one an entire galaxy. Test: prove that the Selberg class is countable by showing that each L-function is determined by a finite set of data (degree, conductor, root number, Euler factors at finitely many primes). Enumerate the first 100 elements of the Selberg class ordered by conductor. Impact: the mathematical universe of L-functions is countable — there are only as many well-behaved L-functions as integers. Each one contains infinite depth, but there are only countably many of them.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the Selberg class S as the set of Dirichlet series L(s) = sum a_n/n^s satisfying: (1) Ramanujan bound |a_n| <= n^epsilon for epsilon > 0, (2) Analytic continuation to C except for a possible pole at s=1, (3) Functional equation relating L(s) to L(1-s), (4) Euler product L(s) = prod_p L_p(s). Prove S is countable: each L in S is determined by finitely many data because (a) the degree d_L is a positive integer, (b) the conductor q_L is a positive integer, (c) the Euler factors L_p(s) for p not dividing q_L are determined by the Ramanujan bound and the functional equation, and (d) there are finitely many primes dividing q_L. So L is determined by (d_L, q_L, epsilon_L, {L_p(s) : p | q_L}), a finite set of data. Since each piece of data is countable, S is countable. Test: enumerate elements of S by increasing conductor.
directions.title: The L-Function Universe: A Cosmic Census of All L-Functions

directions.description: Godel's incompleteness theorem says there are true statements that cannot be proved. But what if we turn incompleteness into a GAME? Define Godel's Casino: a game where the player bets on the truth value of statements that are independent of ZFC. The house deals cards representing arithmetic statements, and the player must bet TRUE or FALSE. The Continuum Hypothesis is the first card — you can bet either way and you're RIGHT in some model. Conjecture: Godel's Casino has a winning strategy that guarantees expected profit > 0, even though individual bets are undecidable. The strategy: bet TRUE on Sigma_1 statements (they're true if provable, and ZFC is Sigma_1-complete), bet FALSE on Pi_1 statements that are known to be independent (like Con(ZFC)), and bet on the CONSERVATIVE extension for statements that are genuinely undecidable. The expected profit per round is at least 1/3 because at least 1/3 of arithmetic statements are decidable (by the arithmetic hierarchy: the fraction of statements at level n that are decidable at level n is at least 1/3). Test: simulate Godel's Casino with 1000 independent ZFC statements and verify the winning strategy achieves expected profit > 0. Impact: incompleteness is not a barrier — it's an opportunity. You can WIN at the game of undecidability.
directions.proof_strategy: Define Godel's Casino: each round, the house presents a statement phi in the language of arithmetic. The player bets TRUE or FALSE. If ZFC proves phi, TRUE wins. If ZFC proves not-phi, FALSE wins. If phi is independent of ZFC, BOTH bets win (the player gets their stake back plus a bonus). Strategy: bet TRUE on Sigma_1 statements, FALSE on negations of Con(ZFC) and similar independent Pi_1 statements. Prove expected profit > 0: by the arithmetic hierarchy, Sigma_1 statements are decidable (true iff provable). For a random statement at level n, the probability of decidability is at least 1/3 (by counting). So E[profit] >= (1/3) * (stake) > 0. The key: even though individual bets are undecidable, the AGGREGATE strategy is profitable because most arithmetic statements ARE decidable. Test: simulate with 1000 randomly generated arithmetic statements at various levels of the hierarchy.
directions.title: Godel's Casino: Incomplete but Winnable Games

directions.description: The Ahlswede--Daykin (AD) inequality states that for functions f₁, f₂, f₃, f₄ on a distributive lattice L, the product of their expectations is ≤ the expectation of their product. This conjecture proposes that equality holds if and only if L is isomorphic to a direct product of two distributive lattices L₁ × L₂, and each function f_i factors as f_i(x,y) = g_i(x)·h_i(y) for x ∈ L₁, y ∈ L₂, with g_i and h_i being non-negative. This resolves a half-century-old open problem and connects structural rigidity in combinatorial inequalities to tensor product decompositions of functions.

directions.description: This conjecture proposes that every prime-order {-1,0,1}-diagonalizable graph must be isomorphic to either a complete multipartite graph with specific parameters or a regular graph with a particular eigenvalue structure. The proof strategy involves leveraging the structure theorem from the provided paper, which characterizes prime-order graphs via their Laplacian eigenvalues and eigenvector properties, combined with exhaustive computational enumeration to handle edge cases and boundary conditions. The conjecture bridges the gap between spectral graph theory and combinatorial matrix theory, with domain bridges to linear algebra (eigenspace decomposition) and graph isomorphism algorithms.

directions.description: For fixed integers $3\le s<r$ and a $K_s$‑density $t$ in the positive range of the multipartite edge‑to‑clique profile, any graphon $W$ that attains the minimal possible $K_r$‑density among all graphons with $K_s$‑density $t$ is, up to measure‑preserving relabeling, equal to the balanced complete $k$‑partite graphon whose part sizes are determined by the classical multipartite construction.  This conjecture extends the stability result of Reiher, Treglown, and Treglown to a full uniqueness statement for all interior points on the positive branch.
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
theorem higher_order_clique_uniqueness {r s : ℕ} (hr :  archaeology \le s) (hs : s < r) {t : ℝ} (ht_pos : 0 < t) (ht_leq : t ≤ 1) :
  ∀ (W : Graphon),
    density W (complete_graph s) = t →
    density W (complete_graph r) = minimal_density s r t →
    W =ᵐᵖ balanced_partite_graphon s r t
directions.proof_strategy: The conjecture can be attacked by first establishing a strong local stability lemma: any graphon with $K_s$‑density $t$ and $K_r$‑density close to the lower envelope must be close (in cut direct) to the multipartite extremal graphon.  One then shows that any graphon achieving the lower bound must lie inside every neighbourhood of the extremal family, which implies equality up to a measure‑preserving transformation.  This may be formalised in Lean by proving that the semidefinite program encoding the extremal problem has a unique optimal solution and by using the regularity‑plus‑sampling machinery hyperlink with the flag algebra framework to exclude any non‑multipartite extremal structure.
directions.title: Uniqueness of Extremal Graphons in the Higher‑Order Clique Density Theorem

directions.description: The paper proves that for any d-regular graph G on n vertices with d ≤ n^{1/12-ε} and any integer vector q=(q_0,…,q_d) satisfying ∑ q_i = n, ∑ i q_i ≡ 0 (mod 2), and |q_i - n/(d+1)| ≤ 1 for all i, there exists a spanning subgraph H ⊆ G with m(H,i)=q_i exactly. We conjecture that this exact prescription holds for every d-regular graph on n vertices and every such admissible q, i.e., without the restriction d ≤ n^{1/12-ε}.

directions.proof_strategy: Refine the anti-diagonal edge-move correction step by replacing the twofold prefix norm bound with a potential that remains O(d^2√n) or smaller for d up to n^{1/2} or beyond, possibly using iterative absorption, balanced random adjustments, or hypergraph container methods to control the lattice cost uniformly for all d.
directions.title: Exact degree-count prescription without polynomial-range restriction

directions.description: We conjecture that the hereditary class of cographs, i.e., graphs with no induced path on four vertices (P4), is generalized spectrally closed: any graph generalized cospectral with a cograph must itself be a cograph. This extends the paper's proven results for threshold graphs (Forb(2K2,P4,C4)) and chain graphs.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem cographs_genspec_closed (V : Type*) [Fintype V] (G H : SimpleGraph V) (hG : IsCograph G) (h_eq : generalizedSpectrum G = generalizedSpectrum H) : IsCograph H := by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Utilize the paper's β-closed walk expansion and the sufficient condition via a walk-realizable {P4}-supporter. Reduce the search to a linear programming feasibility problem for coefficients of β-closed walk counts. Compute a concrete finite witness (e.g., with bounded walk length) satisfying the LP, then formalize the induced-subgraph expansion and supporter criterion in Lean 4 to verify the implication.
directions.title: Generalized spectral closedness of cographs (Forb(P4))

directions.description: For every positive integer d there exists integers k ≥ 3 and ℓ with ℓ ≥ ⌈k/2⌉ and ℓ ≤ k-2 such that the single-degree Turán spectrum Π^k_ℓ contains an algebraic number whose minimal polynomial over ℚ has degree at least d.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem arbitrarily_high_degree {d : ℕ} : ∃ (k ℓ : ℕ), 3 ≤ k ∧ ℓ ≥ (k+1)/2 ∧ ℓ ≤ k-2 ∧ ∃ (α : ℝ), MinimalPolynomialDegree α ≥ d ∧ α ∈ Π^k_ℓ
directions.proof_strategy: Construct an infinite sequence of tree suspensions whose associated transfer functions generate algebraic numbers with increasingly large minimal polynomial degree.
directions.title: Arbitrarily high-degree algebraic numbers in single-degree Turán spectra

directions.description: A biserial algebra Λ is representation-finite if and only if the magnitude of its module category equals the rank of its Grothendieck group, i.e., MagnitudeOfModuleCat(Λ) = rank(K₀(mod-Λ)). This provides a purely homological characterization of representation-finiteness in terms of the interplay between the Auslander-Reiten quiver's Euler characteristic and the Grothendieck group structure.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem biserial_representation_finite_characterization (Λ : Type*) [algebra k Λ] [representation_finite Λ] [biserial Λ] : magnitude_of_module_category Λ = rank (grothendieck_group (module_category Λ))
directions.proof_strategy: Verify the conjecture for classes of biserial algebras where both magnitude and Grothendieck rank are computable: (1) Hereditary biserial algebras (where magnitude relates to Dynkin type), (2) Self-injective biserial algebras (where Coxeter duality provides constraints), (3) Use induction on the complexity of the Auslander-Reiten quiver structure. The key is establishing that representation-finiteness creates a perfect matching between indecomposable modules and Grothendieck group generators, reflected in the magnitude calculation.
directions.title: Characterization of representation-finite biserial algebras via magnitude and Grothendieck rank

directions.description: For every intersecting-union family F ⊆ 2^{[n]}, the Lubell sum L(F) = Σ_{A∈F} (n choose |A|)^{-1} satisfies L(F) ≤ (n+1)/6. Moreover, equality holds iff n is divisible by 3 and F is isomorphic to the family of all n/3-subsets containing a fixed element, or n ≡ 1,2 (mod 3) and F consists of all subsets of size ⌊n/3⌋ or ⌈n/3⌉ containing a fixed element (with appropriate multiplicities).
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem lubell_bound_IU_family {n : ℕ} (F : Finset (Fin n)) (h_inter : ∀ (s t : Finset (Fin n)), s ∈ F → t ∈ F → s.inter t ≠ ∅) (h_union : ∀ (s t : Finset (Fin n)), s ∈ F → t ∈ F → s.union t ≠ Set.univ) : (∑ s in F, (1 : ℝ) / ((n.choose s.card : ℝ))) ≤ ((n + 1 : ℝ) / 6) := by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Use the p-biased μ_p measure on the Boolean lattice to bound the weighted sum Σ_{A∈F} p^{|A|}(1-p)^{n-|A|} for each p∈[0,1], integrate over p to recover the Lubell sum, and optimize the resulting integral to obtain the constant 1/6; extremal families are identified by analyzing equality conditions in the integral estimates.
directions.title: Sharp Lubell bound for intersecting-union families with extremal characterization

directions.description: Let Sh_G be a Shimura variety of Hodge type with μ-ordinary Mantovan Igusa variety Ig_μ. Let D = ⊕_{i=1}^n D_i be the graded algebra of rank one Maass--Shimura differential operators on Ig_μ. Conjecture: There exists an explicit n-dimensional commutative formal group F_D such that the action of D integrates to an action of F_D on Ig_μ, and the coordinate ring of F_D is canonically isomorphic to the symmetric algebra Sym(D) equipped with a specific coproduct structure determined by the Hodge embedding data. Moreover, this isomorphism is equivariant for the natural action of the derived Hecke algebra H^*(K_p, G) where K_p is a hyperspecial maximal subgroup.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem formal_group_integration {G : Type} [h : shimura_variety_of_hodge_type G] (Ig : igusa_variety μ_ordinary G) : ∃ (F : formal_group h.dimension), integrable_action F Ig ∧ Sym (differential_operators Ig) ≃ₐ[log] coordinate_ring F
directions.proof_strategy: Construct the formal group via the universal property of the tangent space of Ig_μ, use the Hodge type embedding to identify the differential operators with components of the logarithm map, then prove the coproduct compatibility by analyzing the group structure on Ig_μ via p-adic Fourier theory and the Mantovan correspondence.
directions.title: Explicit Formal Group Integrating p-adic Maass--Shimura Operators for Hodge Type Shimura Varieties

directions.description: For every prime power q and every pair of integers n, k with 2·k ≤ n, any constant‑dimension Schubert subspace code of minimum subspace distance 2·k satisfies |C| ≤ S(q, n, k), where S(q, n, k) denotes the maximum size of a partial k‑spread in PG(n‑1, q). Moreover, equality holds if and only if the code is a spread code (i.e., the codewords form a partition of the ambient vector space). This conjecture is falsifiable: a single counterexample— a Schubert code of distance 2·k whose cardinality strictly exceeds S(q, n, k)— would refute it.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem no_larger_than_spread {q n k : ℕ} (hq : 0 < q) (hk : k ∣ n) (h2k : 2*k ≤ n) : ¬ ∃ (C : Set (Subspace (Fin n → ℕ))), size C > maximal_partial_spread_size q n k
directions.proof_strategy: combinatorial counting via chromatic and clique obstructions in powers of q‑Johnson graphs, combined with a double‑counting argument relating code size to partial spreads
directions.title: No Schubert code can exceed the size of a maximal partial spread in the extremal distance case

directions.description: Conjecture: For any finite simple graphs G and H on a common vertex set V, if H is a forest, then the analytic spread of the determinantal ideal J_{G,H} equals the rank of the linear matroid M_{G,H} constructed from the incidence matrix of G restricted to edges of H. This extends the proven single-edge case (where analytic spread equals rank of G in Kalai's 2-hyperconnectivity matroid) and predicts equality in the forest case.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem analytic_spread_forest_H {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G H : SimpleGraph V) (hH : IsForest H) (k : ℕ) (F : Field k) : analyticSpread (determinantalIdeal G H) = matroidRank (linearMatroidOfPair G H) H.edgeSet := by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: 1. Formalize determinantal ideal J_{G,H} in Lean using mathlib's commutative algebra and graph theory. 2. Define analytic spread as dimension of special fiber ring. 3. Define linear matroid M_{G,H} from incidence matrix of G over a perfect field. 4. Prove by induction on number of edges of H: base case |E(H)|=1 known from paper. For forest H, decompose into single edges; use exact sequences or properties of reductions of determinantal ideals to show that adding an edge increases both analytic spread and matroid rank by 1, preserving equality. 5. Bridge to existing matroid theory API in mathlib (or develop minimal matroid library).
directions.title: Analytic spread equals linear matroid rank for forest H

directions.description: For a cuspidal automorphic representation π of PGL₂ over a function field F of a curve X over F_q with conductor Σ being a single point with multiplicity 2, the self-intersection number of the corresponding Heegner-Drinfeld cycle on the moduli space of shtukas with level Γ₀(2) is non-zero, implying the second derivative of the base change L-function L_{F'/F}(π, s) at s=1/2 is non-zero.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem heegner_intersection_nonzero (X : Curve) (pi : AutomorphicRepresentation PGL2) (Sigma : Divisor X) (hSigma : Sigma = 2 • point x) : ∃ (cycle : HeegnerCycle X pi Sigma), cycle.self_intersection ≠ 0
directions.proof_strategy: Apply the higher Gross-Zagier formula from the paper, analyzing the geometry of moduli spaces at non-square-free levels, specifically focusing on singularity structures of integral models and their cohomological properties to compute the intersection number.
directions.title: Non-vanishing of Heegner-Drinfeld self-intersection at deeper level

catalog_references: Buchanan et al., Journal of Graph Theory 2026
directions.description: We conjecture that for all integers $r\ge2$ and $n\ge r+1$, the minimum number $b_{r+1}(n+1)$ of complete $(r+1)\!$-partite $(r+1)\!$-graphs needed to odd‑cover the complete $(r+1)\!$-uniform hypergraph $K_{n+1}^{(r+1)}$ equals the minimum number $b_{r}(n)$ of complete $r$\!‑partite $r$\!‑graphs needed to odd‑cover $K_n^{(r)}$. In symbols, $$b_{r+1}(n+1)=b_{r}(n)\,.$$
domain_bridges: construction of odd covers via bipartite subgraph complementations

theorem odd_cover_recurrence (r n : ℕ) (hr : 2 ≤ r) (hn : r + 1 ≤ n + 1) : b (r + 1) (n + 1) = b r n := by
  -- Formalisation of the conjectured recurrence.
  -- Define b_m(n) as the minimum size of an odd cover of K_n^{(m)}.
  -- Show both directions using the shifting construction and the $\mathbb{F}_2$ rank bound.
  admit
directions.proof_strategy: Extend the proof of $b_3(n+1)=b_2(n)$ to arbitrary uniformity.  Develop a systematic 'shifting' construction that lifts an optimal odd cover of $K_n^{(r)}$ to an odd cover of $K_{n+1}^{(r+1)}$ of the same size, showing $b_{r+1}(n+1)\le b_r(n)$.  Simultaneously, apply the $\mathbb{F}_2$ rank bound $b_r(G)\ge r_2(A_G)/2$ to complete $(r+1)\!$-uniform hypergraphs to obtain $b_{r+1}(n+1)\ge b_r(n)$.  Together these give equality.  The combinatorial details involve analysing the adjacency tensors of complete hypergraphs over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and using induction on $r$.
directions.title: Recursive relation for odd cover numbers of complete hypergraphs

directions.description: For the complete graph K_n with n ≥ 4 vertices, the multiset partition dimension equals n-1. This conjecture asserts that the newly introduced multiset partition dimension parameter for complete graphs follows the exact formula mpd(K_n) = n-1, which would characterize these fundamental graphs within the lower bound framework established in the paper (mpd(G) ≥ 4 for connected graphs with at least 2 vertices).
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem multiset_partition_dimension_complete_graph (n : ℕ) (h : 4 ≤ n) : mpd (completeGraph n) = n - 1
directions.proof_strategy: Establish tightness of the lower bound mpd(G) ≥ 4 by constructing an optimal resolving multiset partition with exactly n-1 parts for K_n when n ≥ 4. Show that any partition with fewer than n-1 parts fails to distinguish some pair of vertices due to their symmetric distance properties in the complete graph structure, leveraging the proof technique from the paper's main theorem to demonstrate that the constructed partition is indeed resolving.
directions.title: Exact Multiset Partition Dimension of Complete Graphs

Greenberg's conjecture on triviality of X_K

directions.description: For a totally real number field F and its cyclotomic Z_p^d-extension F_∞ (d ≥ 2, p odd), if there exists a finite subextension F_n such that the natural map on even K-groups K_{2n}(F_n) → K_{2n}(F_∞) has non-trivial kernel, then the maximal pseudo-null submodule X_{F_∞}^0 of the inverse limit module must be non-zero.

directions.description: We conjecture that for any integers r≥2, s≥2 and any n‑ vertex r‑uniform hypergraph H with matching number ν(H)< s, the spectral radius ρ(H) (defined as the Perron‑Frobenius eigenvalue of its adjacency tensor) satisfies ρ(H)≤ρ(十₁(s‑1)(n)), where 十₁(a)(n) denotes the family of all r‑subsets of [n] intersecting a fixed set of size a (the “star” hypergraph). Moreover, equality holds if and only if H is isomorphic to 十₁(s‑1)(n). This is a spectral analogue of the Erdős‑Matching Conjecture, extending the result of the paper to all n (not just “sufficiently large”) and providing a precise, formalizable statement suitable for verification in Lean 4.
domain_bridges: Lean formalization of hypergraphs and spectral radius

1. Formalize r‑uniform hypergraphs as subsets of ℓ[n] {r} in Lean.
2. Define the adjacency tensor and the spectral radius via the Perron‑Frobenius eigenvalue (using existing Lean spectral theory libraries).
3. Implement the shifting operation and prove its monotonicity for the spectral radius.
4. Derive spectral upper bounds via hypergraph decomposition and tensor variational formulas.
5. Analyse the structure of shifted‑saturated hypergraphs with ν(H)< s, showing they must be exactly 十₁(s‑1)(n).
6. Extend the bound to arbitrary hypergraphs using stability arguments.
7. Formalise the conjecture as a theorem in Lean, with auxiliary lemmas for matching number, star hypergraph construction, and isomorphism testing.
directions.title: Spectral Extremal Conjecture for Hypergraphs with Bounded Matching Number

directions.description: This conjecture addresses the challenge of obtaining improved norm bounds for sparse random tensors with independent entries, building on the techniques used in the proof of the spectral gap for random hypergraphs. Specifically, it aims to remove logarithmic factors in the norm bounds, which is a significant open problem in the field. The conjecture is formalized in Lean 4 using the `NormBoundTensor` theorem, which states that for a random tensor with independent entries and a given bound on the maximum entry size, the expected 2-norm can be bounded without logarithmic factors.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem NormBoundTensor {n : ℕ} {r : ℕ} {M : ℝ} (ht : M > 0) (hts : ∀ X : Tensor n r, X.ℓ2 ≤ M) : (∑ X : Tensor n r, X.ℓ2 ^ 2 * X.prob) ^ 0.5 ≤ √2 * ∑ X : Tensor n r, X.ℓ2 * X.prob + M
directions.proof_strategy: The proof strategy involves using the explicit decomposition of an associated selector process, inspired by Talagrand's generic decomposition theorem, to obtain improved norm bounds for sparse random tensors. This approach requires a careful analysis of the variance of the tensor norm and the use of truncation inequalities to control the contribution of large entries.
directions.title: Improved Norm Bounds for Sparse Random Tensors with Independent Entries

directions.description: For every connected simple graph G, the natural homomorphism Aut(G) → Aut(X_G) induced by the action on the network realignment complex X_G is an isomorphism. In particular, every automorphism of the cubical complex X_G is induced by a relabelling of the vertices of G.
domain_bridges: connects graph symmetries to topological automorphism groups
links equivariant homotopy theory with combinatorial enumeration
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem aut_X_G_eq_aut_G (G : SimpleGraph V) (h : Connected G) : Aut (NetworkRealignmentComplex G) ≅ Aut G := by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Use the paper's equivariant generalised Morse theory and the Aut(G)-equivariant strong deformation retraction of X_G onto a disjoint union of a complete graph and a discrete Aut(G)-space. Show that any automorphism of X_G must map critical cells to critical cells, preserving the retraction. Then classify the resulting permutations of components and prove they arise uniquely from Aut(G), generalising the n≥5 case for K_n.
directions.title: Automorphism group of network realignment complex equals base graph automorphism group

directions.description: The paper proves that for c≥2, the number of Dyck paths of semilength n=cm+r-1 whose column-residue class sums are equal (c-balanced) is the Raney number Raney_{c+1,r}(m). We conjecture a refinement: the number of such c-balanced paths with exactly k peaks equals the rational Narayana number N_{(c+1,m,r)}(k) (equivalently, the peak distribution matches that of (c+1)-ary trees with r marked nodes). This is falsifiable by explicit enumeration for small parameters.

theorem peak_refined_c_balanced (c : ℕ) (hc : c ≥ 2) (m r : ℕ) (hr : 1 ≤ r ∧ r ≤ c) :
  let n := c * m + r - 1
  ∀ k, Nat.card {p : DyckPath n // cBalanced c p ∧ peaks p = k} =
    rationalNarayana (c+1) r m k := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Derive the bivariate generating function for c-balanced Dyck paths weighted by peak count using the kernel method extended from the paper, and show it coincides with the known rational Narayana generating function. Alternatively, construct an explicit bijection to marked (c+1)-ary trees that preserves peaks, potentially via the cycle lemma on Raney sequences.
directions.title: Peak refinement of c-balanced Dyck path enumeration

directions.description: Conjecture that any directed strongly regular graph on 108 vertices must have degree k belonging to the set {11,14,22,23,25,34,38,39,41,42,46}. Equivalently, no such graph exists with a degree outside this set.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem no_dsrg_degree_outside_set {k : ℕ} (hk : k ∉ ({11,14,22,23,25,34,38,39,41,42,46} : Finset ℕ)) : ¬ ∃ (G : Digraph 108), DirectedStrongRegular G k := by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Search computationally over all parameter tuples (k,λ,μ,ν) that satisfy the feasibility conditions for a directed strongly regular graph on 108 vertices, and verify that none are viable unless k is in the listed set; then provide a theoretical argument using the parameter equations and transitivity constraints to show that k must belong to that set.
directions.title: Conjecture on the possible degrees of directed strongly regular graphs on 108 vertices

directions.description: Every simple finite graph that is (K₁∪P₄)-free, has toughness at least 1, and has at least 3 vertices is Hamiltonian.
domain_bridges: Formalization of graph toughness in Lean 4
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem hamiltonian_of_K1_union_P4_free_one_tough (G : SimpleGraph V) [Fintype V] (h_free : ∀ (S : G.Subgraph), ¬ S.IsInducedCopyOf (K1 ∪ P4)) (h_tough : toughness G ≥ 1) (h_card : Fintype.card V ≥ 3) : G.Hamiltonian := by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Assume a minimal counterexample by number of vertices. Show that any non-minimally 1-tough graph can be reduced by edge deletion while preserving (K₁∪P₄)-freeness and 1-toughness until a minimally 1-tough graph is obtained. Then apply the structural characterization from the paper (already proven for minimally 1-tough case) to conclude the minimized graph is Hamiltonian, and lift the cycle back to the original, yielding contradiction.
directions.title: Hamiltonicity of (K₁∪P₄)-free 1-tough graphs

directions.description: For every positive integer k, the overcubic partition k-tuple function b_k(n) (with generating function f₄ᵏ/(f₁²ᵏ f₂ᵏ) where f_m = (q^m; q^m)_∞) satisfies the same three fundamental congruences as the classical partition function: b_k(5n+4) ≡ 0 (mod 5), b_k(7n+5) ≡ 0 (mod 7), and b_k(11n+6) ≡ 0 (mod 11) for all n ≥ 0.

theorem ramanujan_congruences_overcubic_k_tuples (k : ℕ) (hk : k ≥ 1) :
  (∀ n : ℕ, b_k (5 * n + 4) ≡ 0 [MOD 5]) ∧
  (∀ n : ℕ, b_k (7 * n + 5) ≡ 0 [MOD 7]) ∧
  (∀ n : ℕ, b_k (11 * n + 6) ≡ 0 [MOD 11]) := by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Show that the generating function F_k(q) = f₄ᵏ/(f₁²ᵏ f₂ᵏ) is a modular form of weight -k/2 on a suitable congruence subgroup. Use the fact that the base function F₁(q) satisfies the three congruences (as proved in the paper for k=1,2,3) and that the congruence properties are preserved under taking powers when combined with the action of the U_p operator in characteristic p. Alternatively, develop an elementary q-series proof by induction on k using the multiplicative structure F_k = (F₁)^k and known congruences for F₁.
directions.title: Ramanujan-Type Congruences for All Overcubic Partition k-Tuples

directions.description: For coprime integers ℓ, μ ≥2, the number of overpartitions R̄_ℓ,μ(n) modulo 4 is congruent to 0 or 1, which are the only perfect squares modulo 4.

directions.description: For the Wenger graph W_5(q) (the k=5 case where the girth conjecture is known to hold), any f-degree fault tolerant 9-spanner must have at least (1/20) * f^(4/5) * n^(6/5) edges for all prime powers q ≥ 2 and all f ≤ q^4 / 10, where n = 2q^5 is the number of vertices. This strengthens the asymptotic Ω(f^(1-1/k) n^(1+1/k)) lower bound of the paper with an explicit constant factor for the largest known explicit construction.
directions.proof_strategy: Use the Szabó-Conlon reinterpretation of Wenger graphs as norm graphs over finite fields. Analyze the number of edge-disjoint paths of length ≤ 9 between vertex pairs that must survive any f-degree fault set. Apply a double counting argument on the incidence matrix of paths versus edges, optimizing the constant via the eigenvalue distribution of the associated algebraic variety.
directions.title: Explicit Constant Factor for Wenger Graph DFT Spanner Lower Bound

directions.description: Conjecture: For every composition α of length r ≤ R, the differential operator ∂_α = ∂_{i1}⋯∂_{ir} acting on the polynomial ring ℚ[X_1,…,X_R] yields a non-zero scalar multiple of the basis element X_{i1}∧⋯∧X_{ir} in ∧^r V, where ∂_i = (1/i!)·(d/dX_i)|_{X=0}. Moreover, the scalar equals the sign of the permutation that sorts (i1,…,ir). This equality holds for all r and can be tested computationally for small values.

directions.description: For all positive integers x ≥ 1 and integers u satisfying ⌊√x⌋ < u < x, the Mertens function M(x) = Σ_{n≤x} μ(n) satisfies the identity M(x) = Σ_{k≤x/u} μ(k)S(x/k,u), where S(y,u) = 1 - Σ_{y/u < n ≤ ⌊√y⌋} M(y/n) + ⌊y/(⌊√y⌋+1)⌋ M(⌊√y⌋) - Σ_{n≤⌊√y⌋} ⌊y/n⌋ μ(n). This conjecture asserts that the main combinatorial formula derived in the paper correctly expresses M(x) in terms of smaller Mertens values and Möbius function values, which forms the theoretical foundation of the O(x^{2/3+ε}) algorithm.

directions.description: Conjecture: For any finite simple graphs G and H, let J_{G,H} be the determinantal ideal generated by the 2‑minors of the generic matrix whose rows are indexed by V(G) and columns by V(H) (as in the paper). Let M_{G,H} be the linear matroid over a field k whose representation matrix is the bipartite incidence matrix of (G,H) (rows correspond to edges of G, columns to vertices of H, with entry 1 if the vertex is incident to the edge, 0 otherwise). Then the analytic spread ℓ(J_{G,H}) equals the rank of M_{G,H}. This extends the known result for H = K₂, where the analytic spread of the binomial edge ideal J_G equals the rank of G in Kalai's 2‑hyperconnectivity matroid.

Show that the special fiber ring S/J_{G,H} ⊗_k k[m] has the same Hilbert function as the face ring of that complex, hence its Krull dimension (the analytic spread) equals dim(Δ)+1. 3. For a squarefree simplicial complex, dim(Δ)+1 equals the size of the largest face, which is the rank of the represented matroid. 4. Conclude ℓ(J_{G,H}) = rank(M_{G,H}).

Specifically, each cluster picture in the complete list associated to a reduction type corresponds to exactly one Weierstrass model, and every smooth projective genus 2 curve over K with that reduction type realizes each of its listed cluster pictures through some minimal Weierstrass equation. Moreover, the valuation of the discriminant and the Birch-Swinnerton-Dyer fudge factor are constant across all Weierstrass models realizing the same cluster picture.

directions.description: For any tree T with n ≥ 2 vertices, the multiset partition dimension mpd(T) equals 4 if and only if T contains at least two leaves whose distance from each other is at least 3. This conjecture refines the general lower bound of 4 by providing a complete characterization for the extremal case in trees, extending the result that mpd(G) ≥ 4 for all connected graphs with at least two vertices.

directions.proof_strategy: The forward direction can be established by contradiction: if a tree has mpd(T) = 4 but all pairs of leaves have distance at most 2, then the distance constraints would force at least two vertices to have identical multiset representations, violating the resolving property. The reverse direction follows from constructing an explicit resolving multiset partition with exactly 4 parts when the leaf distance condition is satisfied. This construction generalizes the proof techniques used for the general lower bound while exploiting the tree structure to ensure the partition is valid. The characterization should be formalized by first defining the multiset representation function, then proving the equivalence via structural analysis of tree topology.

directions.description: Conjecture: Let $p$ be a prime and let $f = \sum_{q\in\mathbb{Q}} [f(q)] p^q$ be a $p$-adic Hahn series with bounded support such that the set of accumulation points of $\operatorname{Supp}(f)$ is finite. Then $f$ is algebraic over $\mathbf{Q}_p$ if and only if there exists an integer $T\ge 1$ such that $\operatorname{Supp}(f)\subseteq \frac{1}{T}\mathbb{Z}[1/p]$ and the coefficient map $q\mapsto f(q)$ is eventually periodic with period dividing a power of $p$ when restricted to each coset of $\frac{1}{T}\mathbb{Z}[1/p]$.

On each translate the coefficient sequence becomes a $p$-automatic sequence; the algebraicity condition then translates into eventual periodicity. The converse direction follows from constructing a polynomial relation using the periodicity and the finite‑state automaton recognizing the coefficient sequence.
directions.title: Order-type characterization of algebraic $p$-adic Hahn series with finitely many accumulation points

directions.description: We conjecture that for any integers r > s ≥ 3, the minimal possible K_r-density among graphons with prescribed K_s-density λ is given by the classical multipartite edge-to-clique profile re‑parametrised by λ, and that the stability theorem holds for the whole range of λ (including the endpoint λ = 0). In particular, there exists a quantitative function φ such that if a graphon W satisfies K_s(W) = λ and K_r(W) ≤ f_{r,s}(λ) + ε, then the cut distance from W to the extremal multipartite family determined by λ is bounded by φ(ε).

theorem higher_order_clique_density_stability {r s : ℕ} (h : 3 ≤ s ∧∧ s < r) (lambda : ℝ) (epsilon : ℝ) (h_epsilon : 0 < epsilon) : 
  let f := multipartite_profile r s lambda;  -- placeholder for the reparametrised profile
  ∃ (F : extremal_family r s lambda), 
    ∀ (W : Graphon), (hKs : K_s W = lambda), (hKr : K_r W ≤ f + epsilon) → 
      delta_cut W F ≤ phi epsilon := by
  -- proof skeleton
  have hpos : 0 ≤ lambda ∧∧ lambda ≤ lambda_max from …
  -- case lambda > 0: apply existing stability theorem
  -- case lambda = 0: prove trivial stability using density‑cut norm inequality
  -- combine via cases
directions.proof_strategy: Build on the existing proof of the higher‑order clique density theorem to extend the analysis to the zero‑density endpoint. Use the existing stability argument for the positive branch, which relies on the first variation formula and the classification of extremal graphons. To handle the λ = 0 case, one must show that the only extremal graphons are those with vanishing edge density, i.e., the empty graph, and that any near‑extremal graphon must be close (in cut distance) to the empty graph. This requires a new quantitative inequality for the K_s-density in terms of the cut norm of the graphon, derivable from the moment method and the known lower bound for the K_r-density. The resulting φ(ε) can be taken linear in ε. Formalizing the conjecture in Lean will involve defining graphons as measurable functions on a probability space, the K_t-density functional, and cut distance, then encoding the inequalities as lemmas that can be proved by induction on r-s.
directions.title: Higher-order clique density stability conjecture

directions.description: The paper proves that every finite simple subcubic outerplanar graph admits a crumby coloring (a red/blue vertex partition where blue vertices induce max degree ≤1 and red vertices induce a graph with no isolated vertices and no simple path of length 3). Outerplanar graphs are a subclass of series-parallel graphs (both are K4-minor-free and have treewidth ≤2). We conjecture that the result extends to the broader class: every finite simple subcubic series-parallel graph admits a crumby coloring. This is precise and falsifiable: a single counterexample series-parallel graph of maximum degree 3 lacking such a partition would refute it.

Define crumby-admissible colorings on fragments with finite boundary states (terminal colors and local red/blue degree constraints). Perform induction on the decomposition tree; prove by hand that a finite family of boundary certificates is closed under composition steps, and use a formalized finite automated verification in Lean to check that all base cases and completed branches yield a genuine crumby coloring. The boundary information stays finite because max degree is 3.
directions.title: Crumby colorings exist for all subcubic series-parallel graphs

directions.description:
We conjecture that the combinatorial condition defining reflected bounded‑growth tuples can be expressed solely by simple linear inequalities and parity constraints on a weakly increasing integer sequence.  In other words, for a tuple \(a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb{N}^n\) the following are equivalent:

1. \(a\) is a reflected bounded‑growth tuple (as defined in the paper).
2. \(a\) is weakly increasing, satisfies \(a_i\le 2i-1\) for all \(i\), and has parity condition \(a_i\equiv i-1\pmod 2\) whenever \(i\) is odd.

Consequently the map \(a\mapsto\prod_{i=1}^n[ a_i+1 ]_q\) gives a bijection between such tuples and the palindromic Poincaré polynomials of type \(B_n\) which do not lie in the image of Stembridge's bottom map from type \(A_{n+1}\).  This yields a purely elementary description of the complete list of palindromic Poincaré polynomials in type \(B\).
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
-- Characterisation of reflected bounded‑growth tuples

theorem reflected_bounded_growth_iff :
  ∀ {n : ℕ} (a : Vector ℕ n),
    is_reflected_bounded_growth a ↔
      (monotone a ∧
       ∀ i : Fin n, a i ≤ 2 * (i + 1) - 1 ∧
         ((i + 1) % 2 = 1 → a i % 2 = i % 2)) := by
  -- The proof is split into two directions:
  -- • (→) Assume \`a\` is a reflected bounded‑growth tuple.
  --   By definition there is a weakly increasing sequence \`b\` with \`b_i ≤ 2i-1\` and parity property;
  --   the reflection argument yields the stated inequalities for \`a\`.
  -- • (←) Assume the linear/parity conditions.
  --   Construct a weakly increasing sequence \`b\` by setting \`b_i = a_{n-i+1}\` and verify that \`b\`
  --   satisfies the required bounds, thereby producing a reflected bounded‑growth tuple whose image is \`a\`.
  -- The details are handled by elementary arithmetic lemmas in Lean.
directions.proof_strategy:
We will formalise the conjecture in Lean 4 by defining the predicate \`is_reflected_bounded_growth\` on vectors of natural numbers, the monotonicity and inequality/parity conditions, and the associated product of \(q\)-integers.  The plan is:

1. Implement the definitions in Lean.
2. Compute the set of tuples satisfying the linear/parity characterisation for small ranks (e.g., \(n\le 8\)) and compare with the known list of reflected bounded‑growth tuples extracted from the paper (via brute‑force enumeration).
3. Use the verification for small \(n\) to gain confidence, then attempt an inductive proof that exploits the recursive structure of \(B_n\) and the relationship with the bottom map from \(A_{n+1}\).

The final theorem will assert the equivalence described above.
directions.title: Characterizing reflected bounded‑growth tuples in type B

directions.description: A biserial algebra Λ over a field k is representation-finite if and only if the magnitude of its module category equals the rank of its Grothendieck group plus one, i.e., Magnitude(Λ) = rank(Λ) + 1. Here, the magnitude of the module category is defined as the magnitude of the Auslander algebra of Λ, which for bound path algebras coincides with the Auslander–Reiten–Euler characteristic N − A + E of the Auslander–Reiten quiver (N vertices, A arrows, E meshes). The rank of Λ is the rank of the Grothendieck group K₀(mod Λ), equal to the number of isomorphism classes of simple Λ-modules.
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
theorem magnitude_characterizes_rep_finite_biserial {k : Type*} [Field k] {Λ : Type*} [Algebra k Λ] [Biserial Λ] :
  (RepFinite Λ ↔ MagnitudeModuleCategory Λ = RankGrothendieckGroup Λ + 1) := by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Use the combinatorial description of the Auslander–Reiten quiver for representation-finite biserial algebras (which are known to be iterated trivial extensions of hereditary algebras of type A) to compute the magnitude N − A + E explicitly. Relate this to the rank by analyzing the structure of the AR quiver components (tubes and Dynkin components of type A) and their mesh categories. Leverage the fact that for hereditary algebras of type A_n the magnitude equals n, while for self-injective Nakayama algebras it equals the Loewy length, and unify these via the biserial structure.
directions.title: Characterization of representation-finite biserial algebras via magnitude

directions.description: We conjecture that the classification of reduction types of genus 2 curves over local fields given in the paper for residue characteristic p≠2 extends verbatim to the case p=2 provided the curve has tame reduction (i.e., the Néron component group of its Jacobian has odd order). Specifically, for a complete DVR R with algebraically closed residue field of characteristic 2 and fraction field K, any smooth genus 2 curve C/K with tame Jacobian has a reduction type among the 106 Namikawa-Ueno families, and the associated invariants (minimal regular normal crossings model, Néron component group, tame conductor exponent, discriminant valuation, cluster pictures) coincide with those listed in the paper's tables for p≠2, with potential stable type equal to the actual stable type.
domain_bridges: Lean 4 formalization of DVRs and schemes

For a family of explicit curves in characteristic 2 with tame reduction (e.g., given by y^2 = f(x) with f separable and odd degree extension for semistability), computationally derive the cluster picture and verify it maps to the expected Namikawa-Ueno label and invariants. Then adapt the authors' p≠2 proof: because tame reduction implies the relevant inertia group has odd order, the wild ramification obstacles in characteristic 2 are absent, allowing the same resolution and component group calculations.
directions.title: Tame reduction classification for genus 2 curves in characteristic 2

In other words, there exists a constant \(C assemblies(r,\Sigma)\in\Q^\times\) such that
\[
\langle Z_{\pi}^{r},Z_{\pi}^{r}\rangle
= C\bigl(r,\Sigma\bigr)\cdot L_{F'/F}^{(r)}(\pi,\tfrac12).\n\]
The conjecture is formulated for all integers \(r\ge 1\) and all finite – but not necessarily square‑free – divisors \(\Sigma\).

directions.description: Conjecture: Let G be a finite toroidal bipartite graph and G' the non‑bipartite graph obtained from G by replacing every degree‑3 vertex by a triangular gadget as defined in the paper. Then the Newton polygon of the characteristic polynomial of G' coincides exactly with the Newton polygon of the characteristic polynomial of G. Moreover, the primitive edge vectors of this common polygon correspond to the homology classes of the zig‑zag cycles of G (and hence of G').

Show that the triangle replacement amounts to multiplying the Kasteleyn matrix by a block‑diagonal matrix whose determinant contributes only a monomial factor, leaving the support of the polynomial unchanged. Use homological analysis of zig‑zag paths to identify edge normals, then invoke the known correspondence for bipartite graphs to conclude equality of Newton polygons. Formalisation can proceed by defining torus graphs, Kasteleyn orientations, and the map from perfect matchings to homology classes in Lean, then proving the determinant factorisation and support invariance.

directions.description: The field with one element F_1 is a hypothetical object that would explain why the Weil conjectures have the form they do — as if there were a field with q^0 = 1 element. Tropical geometry replaces addition with min and multiplication with addition. What if these two ideas are the SAME? Conjecture: The tropical semiring (R union {infinity}, min, +) IS the field with one element, in the following precise sense: the category of tropical schemes is equivalent to the category of F_1-schemes. More concretely, a tropical variety over F_1 is a set with a min-plus structure, and its base change to Z (formally, tensor with Z) is a toric variety. The key correspondence: F_1-points of a tropical variety are the vertices of its Newton polytope, and the 'cardinality' of the tropical variety (as an F_1-object) is the number of lattice points in the polytope, which equals the degree of the toric variety after base change. Test: for each toric variety corresponding to a polytope P, compute the number of F_1-points (vertices of P) and verify that the Euler characteristic of the toric variety equals |vertices(P)| = #F_1-points. Prove the tensor product correspondence: tropical scheme X over F_1 has X tensor_Z Z = the corresponding toric variety. Impact: F_1 and tropical geometry are two faces of the same coin. The field with one element is tropical, and tropical geometry is the geometry of F_1.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the F_1-tropical correspondence: a tropical scheme over F_1 is a monoid object M in the tropical semiring (R union infty, min, +). The base change M tensor_Z Z is the monoid algebra Z[M], which is the coordinate ring of the toric variety associated to M. Prove: if M is the monoid of lattice points in a rational polytope P, then Z[M] is the homogeneous coordinate ring of the toric variety V(P). Prove the point-counting correspondence: #V(P)(F_1) = |vertices(P)| (number of F_1-points equals vertices). Prove: chi(V(P)) = |vertices(P)| (Euler characteristic equals number of F_1-points). This follows from the fact that V(P) is a cell complex with one cell per face of P, and chi = alternating sum of face counts = number of vertices. Test: verify for projective space P^n (the simplex has n+1 vertices, chi(P^n) = n+1), for the Hirzebruch surface F_a (4 vertices, chi = 4).
directions.title: Tropical Dreams: The Field with One Element Meets Tropical Geometry

directions.description: Prime gaps — the spaces between consecutive primes — are like empty cells in a crossword puzzle. The gaps are 1, 2, 2, 4, 2, 4, 2, 4, 6, 2, 6, 4, 2, 4, 6, 6, 2, 6, 4, 2, ... (OEIS A001223). The pattern seems random, but the crossword has rules: (1) All prime gaps are even (except the first gap of 1 between 2 and 3). (2) A gap g can only appear at position n if n+g is prime and all of n+1, n+2, ..., n+g-1 are composite. (3) The density of gap g near n is approximately 2*C_2/(g*log(n)) where C_2 is the twin prime constant. Conjecture: The prime gap crossword is uniquely solvable — given the pattern of gaps up to N, the next prime is determined with probability 1 - O(1/log(N)). More precisely, the conditional probability that the next prime after p is p + g, given all primes up to p, is approximately 2*C_2/g * (1/log(p)) * product_{q prime, q | g} (q-1)/(q-2). This is the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture for prime gaps. But the crossword has a surprise: certain gap patterns FORCE the next number. For example, if the gaps near n are 6, 4, 2, 6, then the next gap is almost certainly 4 (the only way to fill the crossword). Test: compute the conditional probabilities for prime gaps up to 10^8 and verify they match the Hardy-Littlewood prediction. Find forcing patterns (gaps that uniquely determine the next prime) and prove they occur with positive density. Impact: prime gaps are not random — they are a solvable crossword puzzle with deterministic rules.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the prime gap sequence g(n) = p(n+1) - p(n) for n >= 1. State the Hardy-Littlewood gap conjecture: P(g(n) = g | g(n-1) = g_{-1}, ...) = 2*C_2/g * (1/log(p(n))) * product_{q prime, q | g} (q-1)/(q-2) where C_2 = 0.66016... is the twin prime constant. Define forcing patterns: a sequence of gaps g_{-k}, ..., g_{-1} is forcing if P(g(0) = g | g_{-k}, ..., g_{-1}) > 0.99 for exactly one value of g. Prove forcing patterns have positive density: the pattern [6, 4, 2, 6] is forcing because after primes p, p+6, p+10, p+12, p+18, the next prime must be p+22 with probability > 0.95 (since p+20 is even, p+21 is divisible by 3 if p ≡ 1 mod 3, etc.). Compute conditional probabilities numerically for N = 10^8. Test: enumerate forcing patterns and compute their density.
directions.title: The Prime Number Crossword: Filling the Gaps in the Primes

directions.description:
# Future Directions

This project proves the upper half of the generalized Turán result
`ex(n, K_{a,b}, K_{3,b+1}) = Θ(n^3)` and, as a **connector**, re-expresses the combinatorial
cardinality bound in the language of asymptotic analysis.

## What is proved

File `Catalog/Bridges/GenTuranAsymptoticBridge.lean` (self-contained, imports only `Mathlib`):

* `KabCopies_cubic_of_K3tFree` — the combinatorial core: every `K_{3,b+1}`-free graph on a
  finite vertex set has at most `C(b, b) · C(b, a-3) · n^3 = C(b, a-3) · n^3` copies of
  `K_{a,b}` when `3 ≤ a` and `3 ≤ b` (KST-style double count on a 3-element core).
* `genTuran_KabCopies_isBigO` — **the bridge**: for any sequence of `K_{3,b+1}`-free graphs,
  `n ↦ #{copies of K_{a,b}}` is `O(n^3)` in the Landau sense (`Asymptotics.IsBigO`), with the
  Landau constant equal to the combinatorial constant `C(b, a-3)`.
* `genTuran_density_tendsto_zero` — the probabilistic/analytic reading: the copy density
  `#copies / n^{a+b}` tends to `0`.

## Natural next steps

1. **Matching lower bound (the `Θ` half).** Construct, for infinitely many `n`, `K_{3,b+1}`-free
   graphs with `Ω(n^3)` copies of `K_{a,b}`. The parity subtlety in the literature lives in this
   construction; formalizing it would upgrade the `O(n^3)` bridge to a two-sided `Θ(n^3)`
   asymptotic equivalence (`Asymptotics.IsTheta`).

2. **Extremal function as an object.** Define `ex(n, K_{a,b}, K_{3,t})` as the supremum of
   `KabCopies` over all `K_{3,t}`-free graphs on `Fin n`, and state the bridge directly for this
   parameter (`IsBigO`/`IsTheta`), rather than for arbitrary sequences. This requires a
   `Fintype (SimpleGraph (Fin n))` sup with classical decidability.

3. **General `K_{s,t}` forbidden graphs.** Replace the forbidden `K_{3,b+1}` (and the anchoring
   triple) by `K_{s, ·}`, giving `ex(n, K_{a,b}, K_{s,t}) = O(n^s)` under the analogous
   common-neighborhood cap on `s`-sets. The double count generalizes verbatim with `s` in place
   of `3`.

4. **Sharper constants.** The current constant `C(b, a-3)` is not optimized. Investigate the
   exact extremal constant and whether the KST cap can be tightened for specific `(a,b)`.

5. **Further cross-domain bridges.** The `IsBigO` framing invites connections to (a) incidence
   geometry / the Zarankiewicz problem (0-1 matrices with no `s×t` all-ones submatrix), and
   (b) random-graph thresholds, where the vanishing density
   `genTuran_density_tendsto_zero` becomes a first-moment statement.
directions.title: This project proves the upper half of the generalized Turán result

directions.description:
# Future Directions

This project formalises a **local-to-global principle for coordinate influences**
— the engine behind local-to-global KKL theorems for simplicial complexes and
high-dimensional expanders (Kahn–Kalai–Linial 1988; Bafna–Hoory–Kaufman 2022;
Gur–Lifshitz–Liu 2022; Gotlib–Kaufman 2023).

## What is proved

`Cryptography/LocalToGlobalKKL/Basic.lean`

* `inf_decomp` — influences self-average: `Inf f i = InfSub f j false i + InfSub f j true i`.
* `linktot_decomp` — the total-influence version summed over coordinates.
* `localToGlobal_KKL_cube` — flagship concrete theorem: local total-influence
  lower bounds on both links of a coordinate give a globally influential
  coordinate (`(n-1)·Inf f i ≥ 2T`).
* `abstract_localToGlobal_KKL` — the abstract averaging engine: bridge + local
  KKL hypothesis ⟹ global total influence `≥ τ·(∑ w)`.
* `abstract_global_influential_coord` — abstract global influential coordinate.
* `cube_total_via_abstract` — the cube is literally an instance of the abstract
  engine.

`Cryptography/LocalToGlobalKKL/Explorations.lean`

* `abstract_localToGlobal_KKL_variance` — the faithful KKL conditional form
  (non-degenerate link ⟹ influential coordinate).
* `regular_complex_exact` — exact total influence in regular systems.
* `cube_localKKL_influential_coord_real` — real-valued global influential
  coordinate `2T ≤ n·Inf f i`.

## Natural next steps

1. **The genuine KKL logarithmic bound.** The current global conclusion is an
   averaging (max ≥ average) bound. The full KKL theorem gives an influential
   coordinate of influence `Ω(Var(f)·log n / n)` even when the total influence is
   small. Formalising this requires Fourier analysis on the cube and
   hypercontractivity / the Bonami–Beckner inequality, which are not yet in
   Mathlib and would be the main investment.

2. **True simplicial complexes.** Replace the Boolean-cube model by an abstract
   pure `d`-dimensional simplicial complex with a measure on top faces, define
   links and the induced local functions, and *prove* the self-averaging bridge
   `I i = ∑ links w·Iℓ` from the complex structure (rather than instantiating
   with the cube's codimension-one subcubes). The abstract engine here already
   consumes exactly that bridge.

3. **Weighted / spectral links.** Incorporate the spectral gap of the links
   (high-dimensional expansion) to convert the local KKL bound into a stronger
   global bound with an expansion-dependent constant, following the
   local-to-global spectral machinery.

4. **Variance transfer.** Prove a local-to-global statement for the variance
   proxy `V` itself, so that global non-degeneracy follows from local
   non-degeneracy, closing the loop with `abstract_localToGlobal_KKL_variance`.

5. **Hypercontractivity on HDX.** Formalise the Gur–Lifshitz–Liu
   hypercontractive inequality on high-dimensional expanders, from which
   KKL-type theorems follow directly, giving an alternative route to item 1.
directions.title: This project formalises a **local-to-global principle for coordinate influences*

directions.description:
# Future Directions

File: `Bridges/PageSiegelRefinement.lean`

## What is proved

The file formalizes, and proves in full (no `sorry`, only the standard axioms
`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`), a **conditional refinement of
Page's theorem** on Landau–Siegel zeros, framed as a *connector* between two
areas:

* **Zero location / complex analysis** — the repulsion of real zeros of Dirichlet
  `L`-functions (`DirichletCharacter.LFunction`), packaged as `Repulsion`, and the
  mission's premise `NonRealExclusion` (no non-real zeros near `s = 1`).
* **Asymptotics + finiteness** — the pivot `exists_threshold`
  (`m^{-ε} log m → 0`, from `isLittleO_log_rpow_atTop`) and the abstract
  `repulsion_subsingleton`, which turns a repulsion inequality into a
  `Subsingleton` ("at most one").

The main theorem `page_siegel_refinement` wires these together: for every `ε > 0`
there are effective `C > 0`, `Q₀ > 1` such that the Deuring–Heilbronn bridge
`NonRealExclusion → Repulsion` together with `NonRealExclusion` forces the set of
exceptional primitive quadratic characters (real zero in `[1 - q^{-ε}, 1)`) to be
a `Set.Subsingleton`.

## Honest scope / what is assumed

Two genuinely deep analytic facts are isolated as **explicit hypotheses** rather
than proved from scratch (this is what makes the result *conditional*, matching
the paper's own framing):

1. `NonRealExclusion` — the hypothesis of the statement itself.
2. The bridge `NonRealExclusion → Repulsion` — the Deuring–Heilbronn / Landau
   zero-repulsion mechanism, whose usual proof rests on the non-negativity of the
   Dirichlet coefficients of `ζ(s) L(s,χ₁) L(s,χ₂) L(s,χ₁χ₂)`.

Everything *downstream* of these inputs — the effective constant, the monotonicity
argument, and the passage to "at most one" — is a Lean theorem.

## Concrete next steps

1. **Discharge the bridge.** Prove `NonRealExclusion → Repulsion` inside Lean.
   Mathlib already provides the key positivity input
   `DirichletCharacter.norm_LFunction_product_ge_one` (the `3–4–1` trick); the
   remaining work is the explicit log-derivative estimates and the choice of the
   auxiliary point `s = 1 + δ`.

2. **Replace the `min`-conductor repulsion by the classical `log(q₁q₂)` form.**
   The abstract lemma is stated with `log (min conductor)`; deriving the sharper
   `log(q₁q₂)` version and re-deriving `repulsion_subsingleton` from it would make
   the constant match Landau's exactly.

3. **Non-vacuity via character theory.** Connect `ExcSet` to the Kronecker-symbol
   description of primitive real characters, so that "at most one character" is
   phrased at the level of fundamental discriminants.

4. **Effective `C(ε)`.** The proof currently fixes `C = 1`; tracking the optimal
   `C(ε)` through the bridge would yield the fully effective statement.

5. **Remove `Classical.choice`.** The zero witness is extracted with
   `Classical.choose`; a constructive selection (or `Set.Subsingleton` proved
   directly) would trim the axiom footprint.

directions.description: Hilbert's Hotel has infinitely many rooms, each containing a prime number. Room n contains the n-th prime p_n. The manager can always accommodate a new guest (there are infinitely many primes). But what if the guests want to REARRANGE? Conjecture: For any permutation sigma of N, there exists a rearrangement of the primes q_1, q_2, ... such that the sequence of ratios q_n / p_n converges to 1. In other words, you can shuffle the primes almost arbitrarily and the room numbers barely change. More precisely, the set of permutations sigma for which p_{sigma(n)} / p_n has a limit is dense in the symmetric group (with the topology of pointwise convergence). But NOT every permutation works: the permutation that swaps all even-indexed primes with odd-indexed ones gives q_{2n}/p_{2n} = p_{2n-1}/p_{2n} which converges to 1 by the prime number theorem, but the permutation that reverses order gives q_n/p_n = p_{N-n}/p_n which diverges. Test: compute q_n/p_n for 10 random permutations of the first 10^6 primes and verify that most ratios converge to 1. Find the exact density of 'well-behaved' permutations. Impact: the primes are robust under rearrangement — their asymptotic density is a topological invariant of the permutation group.
directions.proof_strategy: Define a rearrangement of primes as a bijection sigma: N -> N, giving q_n = p_{sigma(n)}. Define a well-behaved rearrangement as one where q_n/p_n -> 1. Prove density: for any epsilon > 0 and any finite partial permutation sigma_0, there exists an extension sigma such that q_n/p_n -> 1. Use the prime number theorem: p_n ~ n*log(n), so q_n/p_n = p_{sigma(n)}/(n*log(n)) = sigma(n)*log(sigma(n))/(n*log(n)). For this to converge to 1, we need sigma(n) ~ n, i.e., sigma must be 'close to the identity' in the sense that sigma(n)/n -> 1. Prove the set of such permutations is dense in Sym(N): for any finite permutation and any neighborhood, extend to a permutation with sigma(n) = n + O(sqrt(n)*log(n)) which satisfies sigma(n)/n -> 1. Prove the reversal fails: sigma(n) = N-n gives sigma(n)/n = (N-n)/n -> infinity. Test: sample 1000 permutations from Sym(10^6) and measure the fraction that are well-behaved.
directions.title: Hilbert's Hotel for Primes: An Infinite Hotel Where Every Guest Is Prime
